items.followUp: How does light intensity affect the rate of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Identifies the rise in photosynthesis rate as temperature increases, up to an optimum.
rubric.description: Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate increases as temperature rises to an optimum temperature.

rubric.why: Explains what happens above the optimum temperature.
rubric.description: Above the optimum, the rate decreases because enzymes are affected.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate falls at higher temperatures, preferably noting enzyme denaturation.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of photosynthesis increases up to an optimum temperature.
Above the optimum, the rate decreases because the enzymes involved are denatured.

items.followUp: What is the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration?

rubric.why: Identifies the Krebs cycle as a cyclic series of reactions in mitochondria.
rubric.description: A cyclic series of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the cycle and its location.

rubric.why: States the main outcome of the cycle.
rubric.description: Acetyl CoA is oxidised, releasing carbon dioxide and energy-rich products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that acetyl CoA is broken down/oxidised, releasing carbon dioxide and energy carriers or ATP.

modelAnswer: The Krebs cycle is a cyclic series of reactions that occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.
In it, acetyl CoA is oxidised, releasing carbon dioxide and energy-rich products such as NADH and FADH₂.

items.followUp: What is an enzyme, and how does it act as a biological catalyst?

rubric.why: Identifies biological detergents as detergents containing enzymes.
rubric.description: Detergents containing enzymes are called biological detergents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying enzyme-containing detergents.

rubric.why: Shows what the enzymes in these detergents do.
rubric.description: Their enzymes break down stains, especially protein stains.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the enzymes help remove or break down stains.

modelAnswer: Detergents that contain enzymes are called biological detergents.
The enzymes, such as proteases, help break down stains on clothes.

items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme-substrate complex is formed.

rubric.why: States the key idea of Fischer’s model: the substrate fits the enzyme’s specific active site.
rubric.description: The enzyme’s active site has a shape complementary to its substrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the specific fit, using the lock-and-key analogy or equivalent wording.

rubric.why: Describes the reaction and the enzyme’s role after the substrate binds.
rubric.description: An enzyme-substrate complex forms; products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that products are formed and the enzyme is available to act again.

modelAnswer: Emil Fischer’s lock-and-key model states that an enzyme’s active site has a shape complementary to a particular substrate.
The substrate fits into the active site like a key into a lock, forming an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged.

items.followUp: What is roughage, and why is it important in the diet?

rubric.why: Defines dietary fibre as indigestible material in plant food.
rubric.description: Dietary fibre is the indigestible part of plant food, such as cellulose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition or example.

rubric.why: States a key function of dietary fibre.
rubric.description: It helps movement of food through the gut and helps prevent constipation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning peristalsis, bowel movement, or prevention of constipation.

modelAnswer: Dietary fibre is the indigestible part of plant food, such as cellulose.
It adds bulk to food and helps peristalsis, preventing constipation.

items.followUp: Explain how water moves from the xylem into a leaf cell by osmosis.

rubric.why: Identifies sugar loading at the source as the cause of increased pressure in the phloem.
rubric.description: Sugars are loaded into the phloem at the source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sugar is loaded into phloem sieve tubes at the source.

rubric.why: Explains the pressure difference that drives translocation.
rubric.description: Water enters from the xylem by osmosis, creating high pressure at the source; sap flows toward a lower-pressure sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing water entry and pressure-driven flow toward the sink.

modelAnswer: In the pressure-flow mechanism, sugars are loaded into the phloem sieve tubes at a source.
Water enters the phloem from the xylem by osmosis, increasing pressure; phloem sap flows toward a lower-pressure sink, where sugars are removed.

items.followUp: Which blood group is the universal donor, and which is the universal recipient when Rh factor is considered?

rubric.description: O negative is the universal red-cell donor (O in the ABO system alone).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for O−, or O when the answer is clearly using the ABO system only.

rubric.description: AB positive is the universal red-cell recipient (AB in the ABO system alone).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for AB+, or AB when the answer is clearly using the ABO system only.

items.followUp: Explain how biology is related to chemistry, physics, mathematics and geography.

rubric.why: Recognises biochemistry and explains its connection with biology and chemistry.
rubric.description: Biochemistry studies the chemistry of living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for naming biochemistry and describing its study of chemical substances or processes in living organisms; award 1 mark for the name alone.

rubric.why: Identifies the application of physics to biological phenomena.
rubric.description: Biophysics applies physical principles to biological processes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming biophysics and stating its connection with physics and living systems.

rubric.why: Identifies the use of quantitative or mathematical methods in biology.
rubric.description: Biometry or biomathematics uses mathematics or statistics to measure biological processes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming biometry/biomathematics and describing its quantitative role.

rubric.why: Identifies the link between biology and geography.
rubric.description: Biogeography studies the distribution of organisms in geographical regions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming biogeography and describing the geographical distribution of organisms.

modelAnswer: Biochemistry combines biology and chemistry to study the chemical substances and processes of living organisms.
Biophysics applies principles of physics to biological processes.
Biometry (or biomathematics) uses mathematics and statistics to measure biological processes.
Biogeography studies the distribution of organisms in different geographical regions.
Bioeconomics studies organisms from an economic point of view.
